title: Angiosperm families with economic importance: Brassicacea…
topicTitle: Angiosperm families with economic importance: Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Four Families You Must Know by Heart

Family identification is applied taxonomy: given a flower, name the family from its floral formula, diagram and diagnostic features. The syllabus names four families — **Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Solanaceae, Liliaceae** — chosen because they cover both dicots and a monocot and feed Nepal daily. Learn each by: **vegetative habit → leaf → inflorescence → flower (formula + diagram) → fruit → floral characters → economic plants**.

## 2. The Four Families — Master Tables

### 2.1 Brassicaceae (Cruciferae) — the mustard family

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Habit | Herbs; annual/biennial; pungent latex absent |
| Root | Tap root; some with storage roots (radish, turnip) |
| Leaf | Alternate, simple, exstipulate; lower leaves lyrate |
| Inflorescence | Raceme |
| Flower | Ebracteate, actinomorphic, bisexual, hypogynous; **tetramerous** |
| Calyx/Corolla | 4 sepals in 2 whorls; **4 petals in a cross (cruciform)** — the family's name |
| Androecium | **6 stamens, tetradynamous (2 short + 4 long)** — diagnostic |
| Gynoecium | Bicarpellary, syncarpous, **superior** ovary; **parietal placentation**; **false septum (replum)** |
| Fruit | **Siliqua/silicula** — long/short two-valved pod with replum |
| Floral formula | ⊕ ⚥ K₂₊₂ C₄ A₂₊₄ G(₂) |
| Economic plants | Mustard (*Brassica campestris* — oil), cabbage, cauliflower, radish, turnip |

### 2.2 Fabaceae (Leguminosae/Papilionaceae) — the pea family

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Habit | Herbs, shrubs, climbers, trees |
| Root | Tap root **with nitrogen-fixing nodules (*Rhizobium*)** — the family's agricultural signature |
| Leaf | Alternate, **pinnately compound**, stipulate, leaflets with pulvini |
| Inflorescence | Raceme or axillary solitary |
| Flower | Bracteate, **zygomorphic**, bisexual, hypogynous (perigynous in some); pentamerous |
| Corolla | **Papilionaceous** — large banner/vexillum, two wings/alae, keel/carina of fused petals |
| Androecium | **10 stamens, diadelphous (9 + 1)** — diagnostic |
| Gynoecium | Monocarpellary, superior ovary; **marginal placentation** |
| Fruit | **Legume (pod)** — dehisces along both sutures |
| Floral formula | % ⚥ K(₅) C₁₊₂₊(₂) A(₉)₊₁ G₁ |
| Economic plants | Pea, gram (chana), lentil (musuro), soybean, groundnut, bean; also *Indigofera* (dye) |

### 2.3 Solanaceae — the nightshade family

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Habit | Herbs, shrubs, small trees; often smelly |
| Leaf | Alternate, simple, exstipulate |
| Inflorescence | **Cymose** (solitary or dichasial cyme) |
| Flower | Ebracteate, **actinomorphic**, bisexual, **hypogynous**; pentamerous |
| Calyx/Corolla | 5 sepals, **persistent** (stays on fruit — the tomato's green crown); 5 fused petals (gamopetalous) |
| Androecium | **5 epipetalous stamens** (attached to corolla) — diagnostic |
| Gynoecium | Bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior; **axile placentation**, obliquely placed |
| Fruit | **Berry** (tomato, brinjal) or **capsule** (chili, datura) |
| Floral formula | ⊕ ⚥ K(₅) C(₅) A₅ G(₂) |
| Economic plants | Tomato, potato, brinjal, chili, tobacco, datura (medicinal/poisonous) |

### 2.4 Liliaceae — the lily family (the monocot representative)

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Habit | Herbs with **underground storage organs** — bulbs (onion), rhizomes, corms |
| Leaf | Alternate or basal, **linear with parallel venation**, exstipulate |
| Inflorescence | Solitary or various (raceme, umbel, spike) |
| Flower | Bracteate, actinomorphic, bisexual, **hypogynous**; **trimerous** — monocot signature |
| Perianth | **6 tepals in 2 whorls of 3** — sepals and petals look alike (tepals) |
| Androecium | **6 epiphyllous stamens** (attached to tepals) |
| Gynoecium | Tricarpellary, syncarpous, superior; **axile placentation**; trilocular |
| Fruit | **Capsule** (or berry) |
| Floral formula | ⊕ ⚥ P₃₊₃ A₃₊₃ G(₃) |
| Economic plants | Onion, garlic, asparagus, aloe (medicine), *Colchicum* (colchicine — research drug), tulip (ornamental) |

### 2.5 Family comparison at a glance

| Basis | Brassicaceae | Fabaceae | Solanaceae | Liliaceae |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Class | Dicot | Dicot | Dicot | **Monocot** |
| Symmetry | Actinomorphic | **Zygomorphic** | Actinomorphic | Actinomorphic |
| Petals | 4, cruciform | 5, papilionaceous | 5, fused | 6 tepals |
| Stamens | 6, tetradynamous | 10, diadelphous | 5, epipetalous | 6, epiphyllous |
| Carpels | 2 (replum) | 1 | 2 (oblique) | 3 |
| Placentation | Parietal | Marginal | Axile | Axile |
| Fruit | Siliqua | Legume | Berry/capsule | Capsule |
| Signature | Tetradynamous stamens | Nodules + diadelphous | Epipetalous + persistent calyx | Tepals + trimerous |

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **Topic 15 → here:** every family character is angiosperm morphology applied (placentation, aestivation, fruit types).
- **Topic 16 → here:** families are natural-classification taxa; floral formulae are the compact language of family diagnosis.
- **Here → agriculture:** Fabaceae's *Rhizobium* nodules underpin crop rotation and soil fertility; Solanaceae and Brassicaceae feed the world.
- **Here → Class 12 physiology:** transpiration, photosynthesis and transport will be studied using these very plants as examples.

## 4. Exam Orientation

### 4.1 Previous year questions

No family-specific question exists in the authored bank (dicot vs monocot was asked in 2022 — Topic 15). Questions below are **NEB-style practice**, clearly labelled.

### 4.2 NEB-style practice questions with model answers

**Q1 (3m) — Give the diagnostic characters of Fabaceae with its floral formula and two economic plants.**
Answer: Herbs/shrubs with **pinnately compound stipulate leaves**; roots with **Rhizobium nodules**; flowers **zygomorphic, papilionaceous** (banner, wings, keel); **10 diadelphous stamens (9+1)**; **monocarpellary superior ovary with marginal placentation**; fruit a **legume**. Floral formula: % ⚥ K(₅) C₁₊₂₊(₂) A(₉)₊₁ G₁. **Economic plants:** pea (*Pisum sativum*), gram (*Cicer arietinum*).

**Q2 (3m) — Write the floral formula of Brassicaceae and explain any three of its diagnostic characters.**
Answer: ⊕ ⚥ K₂₊₂ C₄ A₂₊₄ G(₂). Diagnostics: (1) **cruciform corolla** — four petals in a cross; (2) **tetradynamous androecium** — six stamens, two short outer, four long inner; (3) **replum** — a false septum in the bicarpellary ovary with parietal placentation, giving the **siliqua** fruit.

**Q3 (3m) — Why is Liliaceae placed among monocots? Give its floral formula.**
Answer: **Trimerous flowers** (parts in threes — 6 tepals as 3+3, 6 stamens as 3+3, tricarpellary gynoecium), **parallel-veined linear leaves**, and fibrous/underground-storage habit (bulb of onion) — all monocot characters. Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ P₃₊₃ A₃₊₃ G(₃).

**Q4 (2m) — Which family characters make Solanaceae recognisable in the field?**
Answer: Persistent 5-lobed calyx on the fruit (tomato crown), 5 epipetalous stamens in a fused corolla, cymose inflorescence, obliquely septum'd bicarpellary ovary with axile placentation, and berry/capsule fruits.

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Writing Brassicaceae stamens as "6 polyadelphous" — **tetradynamous (2+4)**.
2. Giving Fabaceae axile placentation — it is **marginal** (monocarpellary).
3. Calling Liliaceae perianth segments "petals" — they are **tepals** (undifferentiated).
4. Forgetting Solanaceae's **persistent calyx** and **epipetalous** stamens.
5. Writing floral formulae without the correct symbols (⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic, ⚥ bisexual, brackets for fusion, G for superior ovary).
confusion: **Tepals vs petals:** tepals = undifferentiated sepals+petals (Liliaceae, monocots); petals are distinct from sepals in the dicot families.
**Epipetalous vs epiphyllous:** stamens attached to the corolla (Solanaceae) vs attached to tepals (Liliaceae).
**Diadelphous vs tetradynamous:** diadelphous = stamens fused into two bundles (9+1, Fabaceae); tetradynamous = six stamens in two lengths (2+4, Brassicaceae).
**Siliqua vs legume:** siliqua = two-valved fruit with a false septum (replum) between parietal placentas (Brassicaceae); legume = one carpel dehiscing along both sutures (Fabaceae).
practice:
Why do legume fields need less nitrogen fertiliser?

**Answer.** Because legumes **make their own nitrogen**. Nodules on their roots house ***Rhizobium*** bacteria, which possess **nitrogenase** — the only enzyme that converts atmospheric N₂ into ammonia the plant can use. The plant feeds the bacteria sugars; the bacteria feed the plant fixed nitrogen, and surplus nitrogen stays in the soil after harvest, enriching it for the next crop (the basis of crop rotation and green manuring). A well-nodulated pea or soybean field can therefore skip most of the synthetic N — the fertiliser factory is already underground.
universalFacts: Mendel chose Pisum (Fabaceae) partly for its clearly distinguishable traits — a family character that shaped genetics.
examples: ***Pisum sativum*** — pea; Mendel's experimental plant (link to genetics).
***Solanum tuberosum*** — potato; underground stem tuber (morphology link).
***Allium cepa*** — onion; bulb; classic cytology material (root tips).
practiceQuestions:
**Short answer (2m):** What is a floral formula?

**Answer.** A **symbolic shorthand** that summarises a flower in one line: bracteation, symmetry (⊕ actinomorphic / % zygomorphic), sex (⚥ bisexual), then the numbers, fusion and arrangement of **K** calyx, **C** corolla, **A** androecium, **G** gynoecium — brackets for fusion, underline for superior ovary, overline for inferior.

Example — Solanaceae: ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G₍₂₎

**Long answer (5m):** Describe Solanaceae with floral formula, diagram and economic importance.

**Answer.** **Habit and leaf:** mostly herbs and shrubs; alternate, exstipulate, usually simple leaves.

**Inflorescence:** **cymose** (axis ends in a flower, later flowers from lateral branches).

**Flower:** **actinomorphic, bisexual, hypogynous, pentamerous**.
- **Calyx:** 5, **gamosepalous, persistent** (enlarges over the fruit — the tomato's green star).
- **Corolla:** 5, **gamopetalous**, rotate or funnel-form.
- **Androecium:** **5 epipetalous stamens** (inserted on the corolla tube), alternipetalous, **didynamous-looking but equal** — actually 5 fertile, included.
- **Gynoecium:** **bicarpellary, syncarpous**, ovary **superior, bilocular with an oblique septum**, many ovules on **swollen axile placentas**, basal placentation style terminal.

**Floral formula:** ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G₍₂₎

**Fruit:** **berry** (tomato, brinjal) or **capsule** (datura, tobacco).

**Economic importance:**
- **Food:** tomato, potato, brinjal (eggplant), chilli (also spice).
- **Drug/narcotic:** tobacco (nicotine).
- **Medicine:** *Atropa belladonna* (atropine), *Datura* (alkaloids), *Withania somnifera* (ashwagandha).
- **Ornamental:** *Petunia*, *Cestrum*.

*Diagram:* flower section showing persistent calyx, epipetalous stamens on the corolla tube, and the obliquely septate bilocular ovary.
keyPoints: Brassicaceae: cruciform 4 petals, tetradynamous 6 stamens, replum + siliqua, parietal placentation — mustard, cabbage, radish.
Fabaceae: papilionaceous zygomorphic flower, 10 diadelphous stamens, marginal placentation, legume, Rhizobium nodules — pea, gram, lentil, soybean.
Solanaceae: 5 epipetalous stamens, persistent calyx, cymose inflorescence, oblique septum, axile placentation, berry/capsule — tomato, potato, chili, tobacco.
Liliaceae: trimerous, 6 tepals, 6 epiphyllous stamens, tricarpellary axile, capsule, underground bulbs/rhizomes — onion, garlic, aloe, colchicum.
summary: Four families carry the syllabus: Brassicaceae — cruciform petals, tetradynamous stamens (2+4), replum-bearing siliqua (mustard, cabbage); Fabaceae — zygomorphic papilionaceous flowers, diadelphous stamens (9+1), marginal placentation, legume and Rhizobium nodules (pea, gram, lentil); Solanaceae — five epipetalous stamens, persistent calyx, oblique bicarpellary ovary, berries and capsules (tomato, potato, chili); Liliaceae — the monocot with trimerous tepal flowers, epiphyllous stamens and bulbs (onion, garlic, aloe). Each is read through its floral formula and diagram, and each feeds, heals or clothes Nepal — applied taxonomy at its most useful.

importantStatements: "A family is a hypothesis of common ancestry expressed in a floral formula."
formulas: Brassicaceae has a cruciform corolla and tetradynamous stamens, four long and two short, and a siliqua. Fabaceae has a papilionaceous flower, diadelphous stamens in a 9+1 bundle, a legume, and Rhizobium nodules.

Solanaceae has five stamens joined to the petals and a berry or a capsule, as in tomato and Datura. Liliaceae is the monocot of the four: six tepals, six stamens, and a superior ovary, as in onion. Parallel veins support that monocot placement.

exercises.question: Match siliqua, legume and berry to mustard, pea and tomato.
steps: Mustard is Brassicaceae and the fruit is a siliqua.
Pea is Fabaceae and the fruit is a legume.
Tomato is Solanaceae and the fruit is a berry.
Onion would have been the Liliaceae case, with no legume.
exercises.answer: Siliqua mustard, legume pea, berry tomato.

**Siliqua vs legume:** siliqua = two-valved fruit with a false septum (replum) between parietal placentas (Brassicaceae); legume = one carpel dehiscing along both sutures (Fabaceae).
keyPoints: Brassicaceae: cruciform 4 petals, tetradynamous 6 stamens, replum + siliqua, parietal placentation — mustard, cabbage, radish.
Fabaceae: papilionaceous zygomorphic flower, 10 diadelphous stamens, marginal placentation, legume, Rhizobium nodules — pea, gram, lentil, soybean.
Solanaceae: 5 epipetalous stamens, persistent calyx, cymose inflorescence, oblique septum, axile placentation, berry/capsule — tomato, potato, chili, tobacco.
Liliaceae: trimerous, 6 tepals, 6 epiphyllous stamens, tricarpellary axile, capsule, underground bulbs/rhizomes — onion, garlic, aloe, colchicum.
importantConcepts: **The formula as fingerprint:** each family's floral formula encodes its diagnosis — read symmetry, merosity, fusion and carpel number and the family follows.
examples: ***Pisum sativum*** — pea; Mendel's experimental plant (link to genetics).
***Solanum tuberosum*** — potato; underground stem tuber (morphology link).
***Allium cepa*** — onion; bulb; classic cytology material (root tips).
universalFacts: Mendel chose Pisum (Fabaceae) partly for its clearly distinguishable traits — a family character that shaped genetics.
importantStatements: "A family is a hypothesis of common ancestry expressed in a floral formula."
importantNotes: Practise writing each formula with correct symbols — formulas carry dedicated marks in family questions.
examNotes: Most-tested: Fabaceae and Brassicaceae diagnostics, floral formulae, economic plants.
Diagram-worthy: papilionaceous corolla (banner/wings/keel), cruciform flower, tetradynamous stamens, Liliaceae trimerous flower.
practice: Why do legume fields need less nitrogen fertiliser?
practiceQuestions: **Short answer (2m): What is a floral formula?** — A symbolic shorthand summarising a flower's bracteation, symmetry, sex, and the number/fusion/arrangement of calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium (e.g. ⊕ ⚥ K(₅) C(₅) A₅ G(₂) for Solanaceae).

**Long answer (5m): Describe Solanaceae with floral formula, diagram and economic importance.** — Habit/leaf → cymose inflorescence → actinomorphic bisexual hypogynous pentamerous flower → persistent calyx (5), gamopetalous corolla (5), 5 epipetalous stamens, bicarpellary syncarpous oblique ovary with axile placentation → berry/capsule. Formula ⊕ ⚥ K(₅) C(₅) A₅ G(₂). Economic: tomato, potato, brinjal, chili, tobacco, datura.
enrichedContent.summary: Four families carry the syllabus: Brassicaceae — cruciform petals, tetradynamous stamens (2+4), replum-bearing siliqua (mustard, cabbage); Fabaceae — zygomorphic papilionaceous flowers, diadelphous stamens (9+1), marginal placentation, legume and Rhizobium nodules (pea, gram, lentil); Solanaceae — five epipetalous stamens, persistent calyx, oblique bicarpellary ovary, berries and capsules (tomato, potato, chili); Liliaceae — the monocot with trimerous tepal flowers, epiphyllous stamens and bulbs (onion, garlic, aloe). Each is read through its floral formula and diagram, and each feeds, heals or clothes Nepal — applied taxonomy at its most useful.

mcs.question: Tetradynamous stamens (2+4) are diagnostic of:
mcs.explanation: Six stamens — two short outer, four long inner — define the mustard family.

mcs.question: The papilionaceous corolla belongs to:
mcs.explanation: Banner + two wings + keel — the pea-flower design of Fabaceae.

mcs.question: Placentation in Fabaceae is:
mcs.explanation: Ovules attach along the ventral suture of the single carpel — marginal.

mcs.question: Stamens attached to the corolla are called:
mcs.explanation: Epipetalous stamens (Solanaceae) fuse to the corolla tube; epiphyllous attach to tepals (Liliaceae).

mcs.question: The false septum (replum) is found in the fruit of:
mcs.explanation: The siliqua of Brassicaceae has a replum between two parietal placentas.

mcs.question: Which family is monocotyledonous?
mcs.explanation: Liliaceae shows trimerous flowers, tepals and parallel venation — monocot characters.

mcs.question: The persistent calyx crowning the fruit is characteristic of:
mcs.explanation: Solanaceae's calyx persists on the berry — the tomato's green crown.

mcs.question: Nitrogen-fixing root nodules with Rhizobium occur in:
mcs.explanation: The legume–Rhizobium symbiosis enriches soil nitrogen — the basis of crop rotation.

mcs.question: In the floral formula ⊕ ⚥ K₂₊₂ C₄ A₂₊₄ G(₂), the ⊕ symbol means:
